name: Treating sinus infection for breath

card.summary: Treating sinusitis or post-nasal drip to improve breath odour; nasal sources are recognised in principle, but no breath-analysis trials have tested it.
card.note: Antibiotics are generally not recommended for mild early sinusitis; long-term decongestant spray use can cause rebound congestion.

quick.overview:
Some people attribute bad breath to chronic sinus infection or post-nasal drip, the sensation of mucus draining down the throat. The idea is that clearing the sinuses removes the odour source.

Reference sources describe bad breath as a symptom of sinusitis and note that nasal odour can come from sinus infection or foreign bodies. They also state that gold-standard breath testing has not been used to check whether treating chronic sinus disease improves halitosis.
quick.mechanism: Mucus and bacteria in infected sinuses or nasal passages may produce odorous compounds, and post-nasal drip is said to contribute to coating on the tongue. Treatments include saline nasal irrigation, topical decongestants, antibiotics in selected cases and, for persistent disease, endoscopic sinus surgery.
quick.risks: Decongestant sprays are not recommended beyond about three days because of rebound congestion. Antibiotics have side effects and most acute sinusitis is viral. Surgery carries standard operative risks.

lead: Sinusitis is inflammation of the nasal sinuses. Wikipedia lists bad breath among its symptoms, alongside facial pain, congestion and discoloured nasal discharge [1]. In the halitosis literature, nasal odour is said to arise from sinus infection or foreign bodies, and halitosis is often described as a symptom of chronic rhinosinusitis, but the halitosis article states that gold-standard breath analysis has not been applied to test this [2].

Post-nasal drip is said to contribute to tongue coating, which is itself the main source of oral halitosis, but no study quantifying this is cited [2]. Roughly 85 to 90 percent of genuine halitosis is attributed to causes within the mouth [2].
Treating a sinus infection for breath therefore means applying standard sinusitis care in the hope of improving odour. No trial testing this for breath outcomes was found.
infobox: Acute or chronic sinusitis, post-nasal drip
Saline irrigation, topical decongestants, antibiotics, nasal steroids, sinus surgery

paras: Wikipedia describes acute sinusitis symptoms as including bad breath, congestion and green nasal discharge, and chronic sinusitis as mainly nasal obstruction with subtler pain and fever [1]. The halitosis article attributes some nasal odour to sinus infections or foreign bodies, citing Rosenberg and Scully, but says no gold-standard breath analysis has examined chronic rhinosinusitis as a cause [2].

Wikipedia reports that most cases are viral and resolve without antibiotics, and that antibiotics are generally not recommended for mild or moderate disease in the first week. If symptoms last beyond 10 days, amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate is considered reasonable, and the 2012 IDSA guideline recommends amoxicillin-clavulanate as the initial choice [1]. A 2018 Cochrane review found no evidence that symptoms lasting seven or more days reliably indicate bacterial infection [1].

Nasal irrigation can help relieve congestion, with tentative evidence in acute sinusitis. Topical decongestants give temporary relief and are not recommended for more than three days, because oxymetazoline overuse can cause rebound sinusitis. Nasal steroid sprays are described as no better than placebo for unconfirmed acute sinusitis, with small benefit in confirmed cases. Endoscopic sinus surgery is considered for chronic or recurrent disease that has not responded to medication [1].

No studies found. No trial was located measuring bad breath outcomes after sinusitis or post-nasal drip treatment. Sinusitis trial evidence concerns nasal symptoms and infection cure rates, not breath odour [1][2].
